subtype: Approach: waiting for the perfect offer [Pitfall]
passage:
Joseph's old pay had been a comfortable number, and after the layoff he decided that anything lower was an insult. In the Pune flat he kept a notepad with the offers he turned down: a team lead job at a mid-sized firm, a product role with a friendly startup, both a little under the old figure.
"Take one and keep looking," said his friend Naveen on the phone. Joseph shook his head. "The right one will match."
Months passed. The savings sank, and the rent came due before the interview calls did. By the fifth month Joseph accepted a role in a hurry, on lower pay than either earlier offer and with worse hours.
Naveen never said "I told you so". He just sent the address of a decent chai place.

qa.q: Which two offers did Joseph turn down?
qa.a: Joseph turned down a team lead job at a mid-sized firm and a product role with a startup.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling when refusing offers below the old pay?
qa.a: Joseph felt wounded pride, treating a lower number as an insult, and that pride pushed him to hold out.

qa.q: What could Joseph have done when the first decent offer came?
qa.a: Joseph could have accepted a decent offer or asked for improved terms, while continuing to look for a better match.

qa.q: How might Naveen have felt watching Joseph's months of waiting?
qa.a: Naveen was probably worried and frustrated but restrained, since Naveen gave advice once and never said "I told you so".

grounding: The passage shows a person refusing decent offers to hold out for the old salary, and later choosing worse in a weaker position.

subtype: Approach: waiting for the perfect offer [Pitfall]
passage:
"You turned down the Noida offer too?" Sabina asked, setting down her tea.
"It was twenty percent less than I was making, Api."
"Tanvir, that was your third offer. The first was fifteen percent less, and you said no. The second was a smaller company, and you said no."
"I'm worth my old salary."
"Maybe. But how much is left in your account?"
He was quiet. "About two months."
"In March it was six."
"Something will come."
"Something did come. Three times."
Two months later, with his savings nearly gone, Tanvir accepted a role paying thirty percent less than his old job, at a company he liked less than all three he had refused. He signed it at midnight, too tired to negotiate.

qa.q: How much less was the Noida offer?
qa.a: Twenty percent less than he was making.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir keep refusing the offers?
qa.a: Tanvir felt he was worth his old salary, and pride made the lower offers feel like a defeat.

qa.q: What could Tanvir have done instead of refusing all three?
qa.a: Weighed each offer against his shrinking savings and accepted or negotiated a decent one while he still had time.

qa.q: How does Sabina see Tanvir's choices?
qa.a: Sabina is worried and frustrated, pointing out that something did come three times while his savings fell from six months to two.

grounding: It shows a young man refusing decent offers while holding out for his old salary, so savings shrink and he finally accepts a worse job under pressure.

subtype: Approach: waiting for the perfect offer [Pitfall]
passage:
When I was laid off last year, I made a rule: I would only accept a job at my old salary or more. It felt like self-respect.
In month two, a hospital software firm offered me a role at ten percent less. I said no. In month three, Devika's company offered me a good team and fifteen percent less. I said no. Devika didn't argue, but she asked, "At what point would you change the rule?" I didn't have an answer.
By month six my savings were almost gone. I was lying awake doing sums. When an offer came at twenty-five percent less, from a company with a long commute and a manager who interrupted me twice in the interview, I took it within an hour. I had no strength left to negotiate or wait.
The job I refused in month two would have been better in every way. I just couldn't see it while I was protecting a number.
— Ganga

qa.q: How much less was the month-two offer?
How did Ganga feel by month six?
qa.a: Ganga felt exhausted and anxious, lying awake doing sums, with no strength left to negotiate.

qa.q: What does Devika's question suggest Ganga could have done?
qa.a: Set a point, such as a savings level or a number of months, at which to reconsider the salary rule.

qa.q: How might Devika have felt when Ganga refused her company's offer?
qa.a: Devika may have felt disappointed and concerned, but chose to ask a gentle question instead of arguing.

grounding: It shows someone after a layoff refusing decent offers while holding out for the old salary, until shrinking savings force a worse choice.
